headline: Great Barrington races to keep Housatonic water flowing as emergency link remains unresolved
dek: The town says an emergency connection is supporting Housatonic Water Works while state regulators require a continuous-service agreement, leaving customers facing a bottled-water contingency and a longer fight over the system’s future.
body: Great Barrington officials are working to keep water service running for customers of Housatonic Water Works while the private utility, the Great Barrington Fire District and state regulators try to resolve the status of an emergency connection. In an Oct. 1 public statement, the town said the temporary connection is supporting the HWW system, but continued use requires an agreement for continuous service between HWW and the Fire District. The town described avoiding an interruption as its immediate goal.

The dispute is more than a routine utility contract. The HWW connection is being used while the company addresses filtration problems in its own system, according to the town. Massachusetts Department of Environmental Protection officials told the town that MassDEP does not have authority to compel the Fire District to keep supplying HWW through the temporary link. MassDEP will not approve continued use until HWW and the Fire District reach an agreement and HWW incorporates that agreement into its operating procedures, the town said.

If the connection ends and HWW cannot otherwise meet the requirements of a Sept. 15 MassDEP order, the company is required to provide one gallon of bottled water per person per day to affected customers beginning Oct. 1, according to the town’s statement. That is a contingency in the order, not an announcement that Great Barrington’s water system has already switched to bottled-water distribution. The town said it is coordinating with MassDEP on logistical planning in case an interruption occurs and would assist state agencies if residents need help.

The immediate problem sits on top of a longer-running water-quality dispute in Housatonic Village, a Great Barrington community. WAMC reported in September, citing an interview with Berkshire Eagle reporter Talia Lissauer, that excess manganese has caused water discoloration ranging from yellow to a dark coffee color and affects about 800 people. Lissauer said she was aware of no health impacts from the discoloration, but residents have continued to seek a durable fix. The [WAMC report](https://www.wamc.org/news/2026-09-03/mass-utility-company-faces-scrutiny-residents-face-chronic-issues-with-discolored-water?_amp=true) also described roughly 16 miles of aging pipe that ultimately need replacement.

MassDEP has already penalized HWW for missing a treatment deadline. The agency said in June that a July 2025 consent order required a manganese treatment plant at the Great Barrington facility by June 1, after an earlier March 1 deadline was extended. HWW requested another extension, but MassDEP denied it and demanded $2,500 in partial payment from a suspended penalty. The [MassDEP notice](https://www.mass.gov/news/massdep-penalizes-housatonic-water-works-company-for-failure-to-comply-with-consent-order) said the penalty cannot be passed on to ratepayers and that the agency would continue tracking compliance.

The town is pursuing a separate long-term path through the Massachusetts Department of Public Utilities. Great Barrington and HWW jointly filed a petition seeking a DPU determination of compensation if the town elects to acquire the private system, according to the town’s HWW resource page. The filing does not set a purchase price or complete a transfer. The Oct. 1 update said the valuation proceeding remains active and that the town is communicating with the DPU, the Attorney General’s Office and state officials about a sustainable solution.

Residents have some financial help while the dispute continues. Great Barrington’s reimbursement program can cover eligible bottled-water purchases, laundry costs and filters or other filtration products, with reimbursement now capped at $1,500 per household. Customers who previously received money may apply for additional funds up to the new maximum, the town says on its [Housatonic Water Works information page](https://www.townofgbma.gov/371/Housatonic-Water-Works-Information-Resou). The program does not resolve the utility’s infrastructure problems, but it recognizes costs residents have incurred while waiting for the system to improve.

The next near-term test is whether HWW and the Fire District can document continuous emergency service to satisfy MassDEP. Beyond that, regulators and town officials must address the unfinished treatment plant, aging distribution lines and the pending valuation process. Great Barrington said it will post additional updates as information can be released. Until then, the town’s statement leaves customers with two simultaneous realities: officials are working to keep the taps on now, while the legal and financial decisions needed to make the system reliable remain unresolved.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Great Barrington water service remains under emergency plan
seoDescription: Great Barrington is working to keep Housatonic Water Works service running as an emergency connection, bottled-water contingency and long-term system valuation remain unresolved.
